subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then score my answer the way an AP reader would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

questions.q: Two protons in a nucleus are about 1 × 10⁻¹⁵ m apart. At this separation the electric force between them is a repulsion of more than 200 N. Which of the following holds the two protons in the nucleus?
options: The strong force exerted by the nucleons, which here is attractive and larger than the repulsion
Gravitational attraction between the nucleons, which is very large at such small separations
The neutrons, which cancel the charge of the protons so that the protons no longer repel
The atom's electrons, whose attraction pulls inward on the protons from all sides
optionWhy: At nuclear scales the strong force dominates the interactions of nucleons. Between nucleons about 1 × 10⁻¹⁵ m apart it is attractive and larger than the electric repulsion between two protons, so each proton is held in the nucleus by the strong-force pull of the other nucleons.

A student who thinks gravity holds the nucleus together picks this. The gravitational force between two protons 1 × 10⁻¹⁵ m apart is Gm²/r² ≈ (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹)(1.67 × 10⁻²⁷)²/(10⁻¹⁵)² ≈ 2 × 10⁻³⁴ N, far too small to balance a repulsion of more than 200 N.

A student who thinks neutrons neutralize the protons picks this. A neutron has no charge, so it cannot cancel a proton's charge; the two protons still repel with more than 200 N. Neutrons help hold a nucleus together only through the strong force.

A student who thinks the electrons hold the nucleus together picks this. The electrons are about 10⁻¹⁰ m away and spread around the nucleus, so their pull on each proton is tiny and does not press the protons together.
questions.explain: At nuclear scales the strong force dominates the interactions of nucleons. Between nucleons about 1 × 10⁻¹⁵ m apart it is attractive and larger than the electric repulsion between two protons, so each proton is held in the nucleus by the strong-force pull of the other nucleons.

questions.q: Which statement about the total mass of the particles taking part in fission, fusion and radioactive decay is correct?
options: Fission and fusion change the total mass, but radioactive decay leaves the total mass unchanged.
None of the three processes change the total mass, since mass is conserved as in chemical reactions.
Each of the three processes lowers the total mass by converting some of the nucleons into energy.
In each of the three processes the total mass changes, while the total nucleon number stays the same.
optionWhy: A student who links E = mc² with reactors, bombs and stars picks this. Mass–energy equivalence applies to every nuclear reaction: in an alpha decay, for instance, the new nucleus and the alpha particle together have less mass than the original nucleus.

A student who carries conservation of mass over from chemistry picks this. In nuclear processes the mass change is measurable: in deuterium–tritium fusion the products have 0.01889 u less mass than the reactants.

A student who thinks nucleons are destroyed to make the energy picks this. The number of nucleons is the same before and after every nuclear reaction; the mass decreases because the products are more tightly bound, not because nucleons disappear.

For all nuclear reactions mass and energy may be exchanged. In each of these processes the products have less total mass than the reactants, and the decrease times c² is the energy released. The nucleon number is the same before and after.
questions.explain: For all nuclear reactions mass and energy may be exchanged. In each of these processes the products have less total mass than the reactants, and the decrease times c² is the energy released. The nucleon number is the same before and after.

questions.q: A uranium-235 nucleus absorbs a neutron and undergoes fission. In what form is the energy released by the fission carried away from the nucleus?
options: All of it as gamma rays, since nuclear energy is given off as radiation
As heat produced inside the nucleus, which then flows outward and warms the fuel
Mostly as kinetic energy of the flying fragments, with some carried by photons
As extra mass of the two fragments, which end up heavier than the original nucleus
optionWhy: A student who thinks nuclear energy is all 'radiation' picks this. Photons carry only a small part of the energy; most of it is the kinetic energy of the fragments that fly apart.

A student who thinks the nucleus produces heat directly picks this. The energy leaves as kinetic energy of particles and as photons; the fuel warms up afterward, as the fast fragments collide with atoms and are slowed down.

Energy released in a nuclear process leaves as kinetic energy of the products or as photons. In fission, most of it (roughly 80%) is the kinetic energy of the two fragments as they fly apart; smaller amounts are carried by the neutrons' kinetic energy and by gamma-ray photons.

A student who thinks more tightly bound fragments have more mass picks this. The fragments have less total mass than the uranium-236 nucleus they came from; that decrease in mass is what makes the energy available.
questions.explain: Energy released in a nuclear process leaves as kinetic energy of the products or as photons. In fission, most of it (roughly 80%) is the kinetic energy of the two fragments as they fly apart; smaller amounts are carried by the neutrons' kinetic energy and by gamma-ray photons.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of nuclear fission?
options: Plutonium-239, after taking in a neutron, breaks up into two medium-mass nuclei.
Two hydrogen-2 nuclei join to form a helium-3 nucleus, releasing a neutron and energy.
A uranium-238 nucleus absorbs a neutron and becomes a heavier uranium-239 nucleus.
A water molecule splits apart into two separate hydrogen atoms and a single oxygen atom.
optionWhy: Fission is the splitting of a nucleus into two or more smaller nuclei, as well as subatomic particles. Here the plutonium nucleus splits into two smaller, medium-mass nuclei (and releases two or three neutrons).
A student who has exchanged the names fission and fusion picks this. Two small nuclei combining into a larger one is fusion.
A student who thinks any neutron absorption by uranium is fission picks this. The nucleus does not split; one larger nucleus, uranium-239, is formed. Fission requires splitting into smaller nuclei.
A student who counts any splitting as fission picks this. Splitting a molecule into atoms is a chemical process; every nucleus is unchanged. Fission splits a nucleus.
questions.explain: Fission is the splitting of a nucleus into two or more smaller nuclei, as well as subatomic particles. Here the plutonium nucleus splits into two smaller, medium-mass nuclei (and releases two or three neutrons).
questions.working: Fission: one nucleus splits into two or more smaller nuclei (plutonium-239 + n → two medium-mass nuclei + neutrons). ²H + ²H → ³He + n is fusion; ²³⁸U + n → ²³⁹U is neutron absorption with no split; H₂O → 2H + O is chemical, with no nucleus changed.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of radioactive decay?
options: A uranium-235 nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei after absorbing a neutron fired at it.
An excited nucleus emits a gamma-ray photon and drops to a lower energy level.
An excited atom emits a photon when one of its electrons drops to a lower energy level.
A hydrogen peroxide molecule breaks down into molecules of water and of oxygen.
optionWhy: A student who counts any nuclear change as decay picks this. This fission is triggered by the absorbed neutron, so it is not spontaneous; radioactive decay happens without an outside cause.

Radioactive decay is the spontaneous transformation of a nucleus into one or more different nuclei, or to a lower energy level of the same nucleus. An excited nucleus emitting a gamma-ray photon without any outside cause is the second kind.

A student who thinks any emission of radiation is radioactive decay picks this. The photon comes from a change in the atom's electron energy levels; the nucleus is unchanged, so this is not radioactive decay.
A student who links radioactive decay with things breaking down picks this. The breakdown of hydrogen peroxide is a chemical reaction: the atoms rearrange, but no nucleus changes.
questions.explain: Radioactive decay is the spontaneous transformation of a nucleus into one or more different nuclei, or to a lower energy level of the same nucleus. An excited nucleus emitting a gamma-ray photon without any outside cause is the second kind.

questions.q: Two protons are held 1 × 10⁻¹⁵ m apart, a typical separation of nucleons in a nucleus. They are then moved apart until they are 1 × 10⁻¹³ m apart, 100 times farther. How does the strong force between them at the larger separation compare with the strong force at the smaller separation?
options: It is smaller by a factor of 10⁴, the same factor by which the electric repulsion falls
It is negligible, far smaller than their electric repulsion at the larger separation
It is equal, since the strong force does not depend on how far apart they are
It is larger, as the pull of a rubber band grows when the band is stretched
optionWhy: A student who assumes the strong force follows an inverse-square law, like the electric force, picks this. If it did, the strong force would stay larger than the electric repulsion at every separation and would bind protons together in ordinary matter. It is exerted at nuclear scales only and falls to a negligible size.

The strong force is exerted only at nuclear scales. At 1 × 10⁻¹³ m, about a hundred nuclear diameters, it is negligible, while the electric repulsion, which falls only as 1/r², is still about 2 × 10⁻² N. That is why protons in separate nuclei, even in the same molecule, do not stick together.

A student who pictures the strong force as a fixed 'glue' belonging to nucleons picks this. The strong force depends strongly on separation: it is large at nuclear scales and negligible at 100 times that distance.

A student who applies the rubber-band picture of the force between quarks to nucleons picks this. Between two nucleons the strong force is exerted at nuclear scales and becomes negligible when they are pulled apart.
questions.explain: The strong force is exerted only at nuclear scales. At 1 × 10⁻¹³ m, about a hundred nuclear diameters, it is negligible, while the electric repulsion, which falls only as 1/r², is still about 2 × 10⁻² N. That is why protons in separate nuclei, even in the same molecule, do not stick together.

questions.q: In one fission reaction, a uranium-235 nucleus absorbs a neutron and splits: ¹₀n + ²³⁵₉₂U → ¹⁴⁴₅₆Ba + ᴬ₃₆Kr + 3¹₀n. What is the nucleon number A of the krypton nucleus?
optionWhy: A student who leaves out the absorbed neutron picks this: 235 − 144 − 3 = 88. The neutron is a reactant, so the total on the left is 236.
A student who does not count the three free neutrons among the products picks this: 236 − 144 = 92. Each neutron has nucleon number 1, so the three neutrons account for 3 of the 236 nucleons.

A student who takes the lower number of the symbol as the nucleon number picks this. 36 is the proton number Z of krypton (92 = 56 + 36). The nucleon number is the upper number, found from 236 = 144 + A + 3.
Nucleon number is conserved. The reactants have 1 + 235 = 236 nucleons. The products have 144 + A + 3(1). So A = 236 − 144 − 3 = 89.
questions.explain: Nucleon number is conserved. The reactants have 1 + 235 = 236 nucleons. The products have 144 + A + 3(1). So A = 236 − 144 − 3 = 89.
questions.working: Conservation of nucleon number: 1 + 235 = 144 + A + 3 × 1, so A = 236 − 147 = 89. (Check charge: 0 + 92 = 56 + 36 + 0.) Errors: omit the absorbed neutron → 88; omit the 3 released neutrons → 92; lower number (Z) → 36.

questions.q: A radium-226 nucleus at rest undergoes alpha decay, forming a radon-222 nucleus. The alpha particle, of mass 4.00 u, moves off with a speed of 1.5 × 10⁷ m/s. The mass of the radon-222 nucleus is 222 u. What is the speed of the radon-222 nucleus just after the decay?
optionWhy: A student who thinks the two particles fly apart at equal speeds picks this. The momenta, not the speeds, are equal in magnitude, so the radon nucleus, with 55.5 times the mass, moves 55.5 times more slowly.
The nucleus was at rest, so the total momentum stays zero: m_α v_α = m_Rn v_Rn. v_Rn = (4.00 u/222 u)(1.5 × 10⁷ m/s) = 2.7 × 10⁵ m/s, in the direction opposite to the alpha particle.

A student who gives the two particles equal kinetic energies picks this: v_Rn = v_α√(4.00/222) = 2.0 × 10⁶ m/s. With these speeds the momenta would not balance; momentum conservation gives v_Rn = (4.00/222)v_α.

A student who inverts the mass ratio picks this: (222/4.00)(1.5 × 10⁷ m/s) = 8.3 × 10⁸ m/s, which is faster than light (3.00 × 10⁸ m/s). The heavier particle must be the slower one: v_Rn = (4.00/222)v_α.
questions.explain: The nucleus was at rest, so the total momentum stays zero: m_α v_α = m_Rn v_Rn. v_Rn = (4.00 u/222 u)(1.5 × 10⁷ m/s) = 2.7 × 10⁵ m/s, in the direction opposite to the alpha particle.
questions.working: Momentum before = 0, so m_α v_α = m_Rn v_Rn. v_Rn = (4.00/222)(1.5 × 10⁷) = 2.70 × 10⁵ m/s → 2.7 × 10⁵ m/s (2 s.f., from 1.5 × 10⁷). Errors: equal speeds → 1.5 × 10⁷; equal K: v_Rn = v_α√(4.00/222) = 2.01 × 10⁶; inverted ratio → 8.33 × 10⁸.

questions.q: In one fusion reaction, a deuterium nucleus and a tritium nucleus fuse: ²₁H + ³₁H → ⁴₂He + ¹₀n. The atomic masses are ²H: 2.01410 u, ³H: 3.01605 u and ⁴He: 4.00260 u (the electron masses on the two sides cancel), and the mass of a neutron is 1.00866 u. How much energy is released in one reaction? Use 1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s.
optionWhy: A student who multiplies the mass decrease by c instead of c² picks this: 3.136 × 10⁻²⁹ kg × 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s = 9.41 × 10⁻²¹. That product has units kg·m/s, not J; E = Δmc² gives 2.82 × 10⁻¹² J.

A student who thinks the whole mass of the reactants is converted picks this: 5.03015 u × 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg/u × c² = 7.52 × 10⁻¹⁰ J. Only the decrease in mass, 0.01889 u, corresponds to the energy released.

A student who leaves the neutron out of the products picks this: Δm = 5.03015 u − 4.00260 u = 1.02755 u, giving 1.54 × 10⁻¹⁰ J. The neutron's mass, 1.00866 u, is part of the products' mass and must be subtracted too.

questions.q: A nucleus of mass M, initially at rest, splits into two fragments of masses m₁ and m₂ and no other particles. Which expression gives the total kinetic energy of the two fragments just after the split?
options: (M − m₁ − m₂)c
(M − m₁ − m₂)/c²
(M − m₁ − m₂)c²
(m₁ + m₂)c² − Mc²
optionWhy: A student who multiplies the mass decrease by c instead of c² picks this. The units would be kg·m/s, a momentum; an energy needs kg·m²/s², so the mass must be multiplied by c².
A student who divides by c², the step for converting an energy into a mass, picks this. Its units are kg·s²/m², not J. A mass is turned into its energy equivalent by multiplying by c².
Energy is conserved, counting rest energy. Before: Mc². After: m₁c² + m₂c² + K_total. So K_total = (M − m₁ − m₂)c², positive because the fragments have less total mass than the original nucleus.

A student who thinks the more tightly bound fragments have more mass picks this. For energy to be released, the fragments must have less total mass than the original nucleus, so this expression would be negative. The kinetic energy is (M − m₁ − m₂)c².
questions.explain: Energy is conserved, counting rest energy. Before: Mc². After: m₁c² + m₂c² + K_total. So K_total = (M − m₁ − m₂)c², positive because the fragments have less total mass than the original nucleus.
questions.working: Conservation of energy (rest energy included), nucleus initially at rest: Mc² = m₁c² + m₂c² + K₁ + K₂, so K₁ + K₂ = (M − m₁ − m₂)c². Units kg·m²/s² = J. Errors: ×c → units kg·m/s; ÷c² → kg·s²/m²; products-minus-parent → negative.

questions.q: The table shows four reactions. Which row shows an example of nuclear fusion?
options: Row 1
Row 2
Row 3
Row 4
optionWhy: A student who has exchanged the names fission and fusion picks this. In this reaction a uranium nucleus absorbs a neutron and splits into barium and krypton nuclei: that is fission, not fusion.

Two hydrogen-2 nuclei (smaller nuclei) combine to form a larger nucleus, helium-3, and a neutron (a subatomic particle). That is fusion: smaller nuclei combining into a larger nucleus. Nucleon number (4 = 3 + 1) and charge (2 = 2 + 0) balance.

A student who thinks any reaction producing helium is fusion picks this. Here a single uranium-238 nucleus breaks apart, emitting a helium-4 nucleus: that is alpha decay. In fusion, smaller nuclei combine into a larger one.
A student who counts any joining of particles as fusion picks this. Hydrogen and oxygen molecules reacting to form water is a chemical reaction: the atoms rearrange, but no nucleus changes.
questions.explain: Two hydrogen-2 nuclei (smaller nuclei) combine to form a larger nucleus, helium-3, and a neutron (a subatomic particle). That is fusion: smaller nuclei combining into a larger nucleus. Nucleon number (4 = 3 + 1) and charge (2 = 2 + 0) balance.
questions.working: Fusion: smaller nuclei combine into a larger nucleus: ²₁H + ²₁H → ³₂He + ¹₀n (nucleon number 2 + 2 = 3 + 1; charge 1 + 1 = 2 + 0). The other rows: neutron-induced fission of uranium-235 (a nucleus splits); alpha decay of uranium-238 (one nucleus breaks up, emitting ⁴₂He); hydrogen burning in oxygen (chemical: no nucleus changes).

In each nuclear symbol the upper number is the nucleon number and the lower number is the proton number; n is a neutron.

questions.q: Which description of an alpha particle is correct?
options: A whole helium atom, electrons included, so it is electrically neutral
Four nucleons, each carrying charge +e, for a total charge of +4e
A helium-4 nucleus, made of two protons and two neutrons, charge +2e
A burst of electromagnetic radiation, with no mass and no charge
optionWhy: A student who takes an alpha particle to be a helium atom picks this. The symbol He²⁺ shows that both electrons are missing, so the particle is a nucleus with charge +2e.
A student who thinks every nucleon is charged picks this. Two of the four nucleons are neutrons, which are uncharged, so the total charge is +2e.
An alpha particle is a helium-4 nucleus, He²⁺: two protons and two neutrons with no electrons. Only the protons are charged, so its charge is +2e.

A student who thinks every emission from a decaying nucleus is an electromagnetic ray picks this. Only gamma rays are electromagnetic radiation; an alpha particle is a helium-4 nucleus with mass and charge +2e.
questions.explain: An alpha particle is a helium-4 nucleus, He²⁺: two protons and two neutrons with no electrons. Only the protons are charged, so its charge is +2e.
questions.working: α = ⁴₂He²⁺: 2 protons (charge 2 × (+e) = +2e) + 2 neutrons (charge 0), no electrons; nucleon number 4.

questions.q: How do the electric charge and the mass of an antineutrino (ν̄) compare with those of a neutrino (ν)?
options: The antineutrino carries an electric charge; the neutrino does not.
They are alike: neither is charged, and each has negligible mass.
Both are uncharged, with masses close to that of a neutron.
Both are photons of gamma radiation, differing only in their energy.
optionWhy: A student who thinks antiparticles are always charged, like the positron, picks this. The antineutrino has no charge, just like the neutrino.
Neutrinos and antineutrinos both have no electric charge and negligible mass, so in charge and mass they are the same.
A student who thinks neutrinos are a kind of neutron picks this. Neutrinos and antineutrinos are uncharged, but their masses are negligible, far smaller than a neutron's.
A student who thinks every emission from a decaying nucleus is electromagnetic radiation picks this. Neutrinos and antineutrinos are particles, not photons; the photon of a decay is the gamma ray.
questions.explain: Neutrinos and antineutrinos both have no electric charge and negligible mass, so in charge and mass they are the same.

questions.q: Compared with the nucleus before a beta-minus decay, how many protons and neutrons does the nucleus have after the decay?
options: One fewer proton and one extra neutron
No change: the same protons and neutrons
One more proton and one fewer neutron
Same number of protons, one fewer neutron
optionWhy: A student who thinks the minus sign means the proton number goes down picks this. That is the change in β⁺ decay; in β⁻ decay the emitted charge is −e, so the nucleus gains +e: one more proton.
A student who thinks the beta particle is an orbiting electron thrown out of the atom picks this. The electron comes from the nucleus, where a neutron changes into a proton.
In β⁻ decay a neutron in the nucleus changes into a proton, emitting an electron and an antineutrino. The nucleus gains a proton and loses a neutron; its nucleon number is unchanged.
A student who thinks the changed neutron is simply lost picks this. The neutron is not lost but becomes a proton, so the proton number rises by 1 and the nucleon number is unchanged.
questions.explain: In β⁻ decay a neutron in the nucleus changes into a proton, emitting an electron and an antineutrino. The nucleus gains a proton and loses a neutron; its nucleon number is unchanged.

questions.q: Which statement about gamma decay is correct?
options: The nucleus becomes a different element as it emits the photon.
It happens first, preparing the nucleus for an alpha or beta decay.
The nucleus absorbs a photon and moves to a higher energy state.
The nucleus loses energy but keeps its proton and nucleon numbers.
optionWhy: A student who thinks every type of decay changes the element picks this. The photon carries no charge, so the proton number, and therefore the element, is unchanged.
A student who thinks gamma emission comes first picks this. Gamma decay follows an alpha or beta decay that has left the new nucleus in an excited state.
A student who confuses emission with absorption picks this. In gamma decay the nucleus emits a photon and moves down to a lower energy state.

In gamma decay an excited nucleus emits a photon and drops to a lower energy state. A photon has no charge and no nucleon number, so the proton and nucleon numbers are unchanged; only the nucleus's energy decreases.
questions.explain: In gamma decay an excited nucleus emits a photon and drops to a lower energy state. A photon has no charge and no nucleon number, so the proton and nucleon numbers are unchanged; only the nucleus's energy decreases.

questions.q: Enormous numbers of neutrinos produced by nuclear fusion in the Sun pass through Earth every second, and almost none of them are absorbed or deflected on the way. Which statement best explains this?
options: They are uncharged, and uncharged particles pass through matter freely.
Their mass is so small that they slip through the gaps between atoms.
They are long-wavelength electromagnetic waves, which pass through solids.
No electric or strong forces act on them; only the weak force and gravity do.
optionWhy: A student who thinks any uncharged particle passes through matter picks this. Neutrons and gamma-ray photons are uncharged, yet matter absorbs them; lack of charge alone does not explain the neutrinos' behavior.

A student who pictures matter as a sieve picks this. Particles are stopped by the forces they feel, not by their size: beta particles also have very little mass, yet a few millimeters of aluminum stop them.

A student who thinks every emission from a nuclear process is an electromagnetic wave picks this. Neutrinos are particles, not electromagnetic waves; they pass through Earth because they interact only through the weak and gravitational forces.

Neutrinos have no charge, so no electric force acts on them, and they do not feel the strong force that binds nucleons. They interact with matter only through the weak and gravitational forces, which give very little interaction, so almost all of them pass straight through.
questions.explain: Neutrinos have no charge, so no electric force acts on them, and they do not feel the strong force that binds nucleons. They interact with matter only through the weak and gravitational forces, which give very little interaction, so almost all of them pass straight through.

questions.q: A beam of electrons enters the region between two oppositely charged parallel plates with velocity v, as shown, and follows track 3. A beam of positrons then enters with the same velocity. The figure shows four possible tracks, numbered 1 to 4 (not drawn to scale). Which track do the positrons follow?
options: Track 1
Track 2
Track 3
Track 4
optionWhy: A positron has the same mass as an electron and the opposite charge, +e. The electric force on it has the same magnitude as on an electron but the opposite direction, so it accelerates just as much, toward the negative plate: its track is the mirror image of the electrons' track.

A student who thinks a positron has a proton's mass picks this track, which curves the right way but only slightly. A positron has an electron's mass, so the same force gives it the same large acceleration as an electron.
A student who thinks β⁺ particles are ordinary electrons picks the electrons' own track. A positron's charge is +e, opposite to an electron's, so the force on it is in the opposite direction.
A student who thinks beta-plus radiation is an electromagnetic ray picks the straight track. Positrons are charged particles, so the electric field between the plates exerts a force on them.
questions.explain: A positron has the same mass as an electron and the opposite charge, +e. The electric force on it has the same magnitude as on an electron but the opposite direction, so it accelerates just as much, toward the negative plate: its track is the mirror image of the electrons' track.
questions.working: Force F = qE: same magnitude for e⁺ and e⁻, opposite direction. Same mass m_e → same magnitude of acceleration → mirror-image track, curving toward the negative plate.

questions.q: A student proposes that a free neutron decays into a proton and an electron and nothing else: n → p + e⁻. Which conservation law that holds in all nuclear decays would this proposal break?
options: Charge, since two charged particles would come from one neutral particle
Nucleon number, since a neutron would be replaced by a proton
Lepton number, since the number of electrons and neutrinos would rise
Mass, since the proton and electron have less mass than the neutron
optionWhy: A student who thinks charged particles cannot come from an uncharged one picks this. The charges +e and −e add to zero, the neutron's charge, so charge is conserved.
A student who thinks changing a neutron into a proton changes the nucleon count picks this. Protons and neutrons are both nucleons: one nucleon before, one after.

Lepton number counts electrons and neutrinos, with a positron or antineutrino counted as −1. Before the decay it is 0; after n → p + e⁻ it would be +1, from the electron, so lepton number would not be conserved. In the actual decay an antineutrino (−1) is also emitted, so the total stays 0.

A student who thinks mass must be conserved picks this. The products of any decay have less mass than the original particle; the difference is released as energy. Mass on its own is not one of the conserved quantities.
questions.explain: Lepton number counts electrons and neutrinos, with a positron or antineutrino counted as −1. Before the decay it is 0; after n → p + e⁻ it would be +1, from the electron, so lepton number would not be conserved. In the actual decay an antineutrino (−1) is also emitted, so the total stays 0.

questions.q: A radium-226 nucleus, ²²⁶₈₈Ra, undergoes alpha decay. How many neutrons does the resulting nucleus contain?
optionWhy: A student who thinks the alpha particle's charge is +4e subtracts 4 from Z as well as from A, giving N = 222 − 84 = 138, the same as before the decay. The alpha particle has two protons, so Z falls by 2 and N falls by 2.
The alpha particle, ⁴₂He, removes 4 nucleons and 2 protons. The new nucleus has A = 226 − 4 = 222 and Z = 88 − 2 = 86, so N = A − Z = 222 − 86 = 136.
A student who exchanges the two changes, taking 2 from A and 4 from Z, gets A = 224 and Z = 84, so N = 140. Alpha decay lowers A by 4 and Z by 2.
A student who takes the nucleon number to be the number of neutrons picks this: 222 is the new nucleus's nucleon number. The number of neutrons is A − Z = 222 − 86 = 136.
questions.explain: The alpha particle, ⁴₂He, removes 4 nucleons and 2 protons. The new nucleus has A = 226 − 4 = 222 and Z = 88 − 2 = 86, so N = A − Z = 222 − 86 = 136.

questions.q: The bar chart shows the numbers of protons and neutrons in a nucleus before and after it undergoes a single radioactive decay. Which particles are emitted in this decay?
options: An electron and an antineutrino
One positron and one antineutrino
A gamma-ray photon and nothing else
One positron and one neutrino
optionWhy: A student who has the directions of the beta decays reversed picks this. Emitting an electron (β⁻ decay) turns a neutron into a proton, which would raise the proton number; here it falls.
A student who pairs the positron with the antineutrino picks this. In β⁺ decay the positron is emitted with a neutrino.
A student who thinks gamma decay can change the element picks this. A gamma-ray photon has no charge, so it cannot change the number of protons; here the proton number has changed.

The number of protons falls from 11 to 10 and the number of neutrons rises from 11 to 12, while the total number of nucleons stays 22: a proton has changed into a neutron. That is β⁺ decay, in which a positron and a neutrino are emitted.
